Chapter 3: Lessons from Successes and Failures
When you’re young, it’s so easy to see your parents as these unshakeable pillars, right? You think they always have the answers, like they never mess up. But as this father writes to Su Yen, he wants to peel back that illusion—he shares honest stories about his own wins and, just as importantly, his stumbles along the way.
Why? Because real wisdom doesn’t come from getting it perfect every time. It comes from learning, both when things go right and when they don’t.
He remembers his very first job—not some dream gig, but something he took because he had to. The work was repetitive, the hours dragged on, and honestly, the paycheck barely covered the basics. There were days he wondered, “Did I just take the easy way out?” But over time, he realized even boring tasks could teach him something. He learned patience, the value of showing up, and how important it is to give your best effort—even if nobody’s watching.
Of course, there were tough moments too. He tells Su Yen about a business venture that completely collapsed, leaving him with more debt than hope and a bruised sense of pride. For a while, shame and self-doubt took over. He worried he’d let his family down. But thanks to the quiet support of people who cared about him, and the understanding that failure isn’t the end—it’s actually a new beginning—he found the strength to pick himself back up.
These ups and downs taught him that success is almost never a straight road. Most folks only see the final result—the new title, the happy family, the comfy house. But they don’t see the setbacks, the sleepless nights, or those moments when you’re just not sure if you can keep going. He realized real resilience is forged in those tough times, not when everything’s smooth sailing.
So, he encourages Su Yen to take risks, to try out new things, and to treat mistakes as stepping stones, not dead ends. He gets it—there’s a ton of pressure to succeed, especially in a world that puts achievement on a pedestal. But he reminds her, true success isn’t about job titles or material stuff. It’s about your ability to learn, adapt, and stay true to what matters most.
The father also reflects on humility. He shares how a friend of his reached incredible professional heights, but ended up feeling isolated and unhappy. That story was a wake-up call: ambition is great, but not if it means sacrificing your relationships or your own sense of integrity.
He hopes Su Yen will remember it’s okay to ask for help, to admit when she doesn’t have all the answers, and to genuinely celebrate other people’s successes. Because in the end, what really counts is not just how high you climb, but how you treat yourself and the people around you along the way.
